analysis.one_liner: Lets student loan borrowers refinance at lower fixed rates, paid for by a 30% tax on millionaires' income.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 35 Senate cosponsors, the bill never received a committee or floor vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let people with older federal, guaranteed-bank, or private student loans refinance at the lower interest rates the government charged in the 2013–14 school year, locked in for the life of the loan. Eligibility would be aimed at borrowers with the greatest financial need, and borrowers with private loans would have to be current on payments to qualify. The cost would be covered by a new 30% minimum tax on each dollar of income above $1 million, and the refinancing program would shut down within two years.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers still paying high rates on loans taken out before July 1, 2015 — federal, guaranteed-bank, and private student loans alike. The bill directs the Education Department to prioritize borrowers with the greatest financial need, and fixes the lower rate for the life of the loan, which can save a borrower thousands of dollars over the years.

how_it_helps.text: Borrowers with federal Direct Loans and older bank-based FFEL loans disbursed before July 1, 2015 could refinance at the interest rates the government charged for the 12 months starting July 1, 2013, fixed for the life of the loan.
Borrowers with private student loans in good standing could refinance them into federal loans at those same fixed federal rates, with the government paying off the private lender directly.
Eligibility rules must be based on income or debt-to-income ratio and must consider providing access for borrowers with the greatest financial need.
The Education Department would run a campaign, with consumer agencies, to alert borrowers that they may be eligible to refinance.
The refinancing programs would be paid for by a 30% minimum tax rate on the income of taxpayers earning over $1 million, with leftover revenue returned to the Treasury for deficit reduction.

analysis.who_pays: Households earning more than $1 million a year, who would pay a 30% minimum rate on income above their charitable deductions. The federal government would also take on the risk of holding refinanced private loans on its own books.

drawbacks.text: The refinancing program is temporary: it must terminate on whichever comes first of the date its net cost equals the new tax revenue or two years after enactment, so borrowers who miss the window get nothing.

Borrowers who refinance private loans into federal loans give up access to public-service loan forgiveness and related repayment programs for those loans, and payments made before refinancing do not count toward income-based forgiveness.
Only borrowers in good standing can refinance private loans; people already in default are excluded.
Borrowers must complete loan counseling before a private loan can be refinanced, adding a step that could slow participation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and direct: borrowers locked into rates of 6–8% or higher would get the cheaper rates the government already offered newer loans, and the bill pays for itself with a tax confined to seven-figure incomes rather than adding to the deficit. The trade-offs are that the program is short-lived (at most two years), that refinancing a private loan means surrendering forgiveness programs that some borrowers may be better off keeping, and that defaulters — often the people in the worst shape — are left out.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to its Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it sat there until the Congress ended, and the full Senate never voted on it.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill in the Senate on March 18, 2015, joined by 29 initial cosponsors.
The bill attracted 35 cosponsors in total — 34 Democrats and one Independent — before any action was taken on it.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day of introduction, and the action record shows no further committee or floor action for the rest of the 114th Congress.
The bill would have created refinancing programs for federal, FFEL, and private student loans, financed by a 30% minimum tax on income over $1 million.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, private student lenders kept collecting the high interest rates on their existing loans, and households earning over $1 million never faced the 30% minimum tax. Borrowers stayed locked into their original rates.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its case for letting borrowers refinance at lower rates.

for.name: 34 of 44 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the backing of more than three-quarters of the Senate's Democratic caucus.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote during the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 35 cosponsors was a Democrat or the Senate's Independent; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-run Finance Committee and Republican Senate leadership never brought it to a vote.

industries.note: Borrowers could refinance expensive private loans into cheaper fixed-rate federal loans, with the government paying the lender off and discharging the borrower — cutting the lenders' future interest revenue. The bill also requires lenders to report default and delinquency data to regulators and Congress, adding oversight of the private loan market.

industries.industry: FFEL program lenders and guaranty agencies
industries.note: Older bank-based student loans would be paid off with federal Direct Loan proceeds, ending the ongoing interest stream those lenders collect on guaranteed loans they hold.

industries.industry: Households with more than $1 million in annual income
industries.note: A new 30% minimum tax would apply to income above $1 million after charitable deductions, directly raising what the highest-earning households pay to fund the refinancing program.

industries.industry: Federal student loan program (Department of Education)
industries.note: The Education Department would gain hundreds of thousands of new fixed-rate loans on its books, collecting lower interest than borrowers were paying but gaining direct oversight of borrowers who were previously in private markets.
